Title: The wars in thirteen sieges
Summary: A short tour of the whole war, from the first sieges of 1642 to one of the last Royalist strongholds in 1652.
Story:
Between 1639 and 1652 war ran through all three of Charles I's kingdoms: Scotland, Ireland, and England with Wales. Most of the fighting was not pitched battle but siege. Towns, castles, churches and great houses were fortified, surrounded, starved, stormed or talked into surrender.

This tour follows thirteen sieges in order: the scramble for ports in 1642, the King's high tide in 1643, the turn of the war at Marston Moor and Naseby, the fall of the King's last strongholds in 1646, the Second Civil War of 1648, and Cromwell's campaigns in Ireland and Scotland.

Newark, home of the National Civil War Centre, appears twice. When you've finished, try the other stories, or click any circle on the map.

Title: The longest sieges
Summary: Ten sieges that went on for months or years.
Story:
Most sieges were over in days. These ten went on for months, and a few for years. Skipton Castle was held for the King for around three years, and Bolton Castle in Wensleydale for more than two.

Long sieges were usually blockades. The attackers had too few men or guns to storm the walls, so they ringed the place, cut it off and waited for hunger, disease or bad news to do the work. Many ended only when the war around them was already lost.

Title: The bloodiest sieges
Summary: Ten sieges with the heaviest killing, from a village church to Cromwell's Irish campaign.
Story:
By the custom of the time, a garrison that refused to surrender and was then taken by storm could expect little mercy. These ten sieges show what that meant in practice: villagers killed in Barthomley church, the sacks of Bolton and Leicester, and Cromwell's storming of Drogheda and Wexford in 1649.

Several are remembered on both sides to this day, and accounts of what happened were fought over in print as fiercely as the sieges themselves.

Title: Women under siege
Summary: Women who held, defended or shaped a siege.
Story:
With husbands away at the war, many women found themselves in command of a house or castle. Lady Brilliana Harley held Brampton Bryan for Parliament, and the Countess of Derby held Lathom House for the King until Prince Rupert relieved her.

Others shaped events in different ways: the 400 women of Worcester who went out with shovels and spades, Lady Wyndham's "love token", a shot fired at Cromwell from the walls of Bridgwater, and the minister's wife who carried the Scottish crown jewels out of Dunnottar under the besiegers' noses.

Title: Must read
Summary: A handful of the strangest and most surprising stories in the collection.
Story:
Ten sieges with stories too good to miss: a son ordered to attack his own father at Faringdon, a captain at Crowland who fired at his own father without knowing it, Dover Castle taken by a dozen townsmen who climbed the cliffs, and Royalists at Portland who got through the gates disguised as fleeing Parliamentarians.

Start anywhere: each one stands on its own.

Title: The King's finest sieges
Summary: The Royalists' greatest siege successes.
Story:
The King's side won its best siege victories early in the war, when Prince Rupert's speed and daring kept Parliament off balance. The storming of Bristol in July 1643 gave the King England's second city and its port; the relief of Newark in March 1644 was one of Rupert's most complete successes.

That summer the Earl of Essex's whole army was trapped around Lostwithiel in Cornwall and forced to surrender its foot soldiers. Later highlights are rarer: the stubborn defence of Pembroke in 1648 and the quick capture of Torksey. Together they show what the Royalists could do when they had the initiative.

Title: Parliament's finest sieges
Summary: Parliament's greatest siege successes.
Story:
Parliament's best siege victories came in two kinds. Early on, its strength was holding out: Plymouth and Hull, kept supplied from the sea, survived everything the King sent against them, and the relief of Nantwich in January 1644 broke the Royalist hold on Cheshire.

Later it was taking: the New Model Army's capture of Bristol in September 1645, the long blockade of Chester, and the surrender of the King's own capital at Oxford, and of Newark, in 1646.

Title: Taken by storm
Summary: Sieges ended by an assault over the walls or through a breach.
Story:
Storming was the quickest way to end a siege and the most dangerous. Attackers went in with scaling ladders, through a breach battered by cannon or a gate blown in, and the fighting at the walls was usually short and savage.

A town that held out until it was stormed had, by the custom of the time, given up its right to terms. Plunder usually followed, and sometimes killing. Prince Rupert's storming of Bristol in 1643, of Bolton in 1644 and of Leicester in 1645, and Cromwell's storming of Basing House in October 1645, are among the best known.

Title: Starved out
Summary: Blockades that ended when food, water or hope ran out.
Story:
When a place was too strong to storm, the besiegers dug in around it and waited. Supplies ran short, disease spread through crowded garrisons and towns, and in the end the defenders had to ask for terms.

Carlisle held out against the Scots for eight months before surrendering in June 1645, and the people of Chester were starving by the winter of 1645. At Pendennis, ships blockading from the sea made the hunger complete, and Colchester held out for eleven weeks in the summer of 1648 before hunger forced its surrender.

Title: Surrendered on terms
Summary: The most common ending: a garrison agreed terms and marched out.
Story:
Most sieges did not end in a fight to the finish. After a summons and a parley, the two sides agreed written "articles": who could leave, with what weapons, whether the colours could fly and the drums beat, and where the garrison could march to.

Good terms were a mark of a well-fought defence. At Greenlands House in 1644 the Royalists marched out to Oxford "fully armed with colours flying", and when Oxford itself surrendered in 1646 the articles protected its university and citizens. A governor who gave up too easily could face his own side's court martial.

Title: Relieved
Summary: Sieges lifted when a field army marched to the rescue.
Story:
A garrison's best hope was relief: an army marching to drive off the besiegers. The approach of a relieving force often ended a siege without a battle, because the besiegers could not fight in two directions at once.

The Earl of Essex's march to save Gloucester in September 1643 was one of the turning points of the war. Prince Rupert relieved Newark in March 1644 and Lathom House that May, and Taunton was relieved three times. Relief was not always the end of the story: the march to relieve York in 1644 led straight to Marston Moor.

Title: The besiegers gave up
Summary: Sieges abandoned by the attackers without a relieving army.
Story:
Sometimes the attackers simply went away. Sieges were expensive, soldiers deserted when they were not paid, local troops wanted to go home for the harvest, and a determined garrison could make a siege more trouble than it was worth.

Hull saw off the Royalists twice: the King himself in 1642, and the Marquess of Newcastle's army in 1643. Corfe Castle and Brampton Bryan both outlasted their besiegers in 1643, and Sir William Waller had to abandon Basing House that November when his London regiments refused to stay. Oxford was left alone in 1645 when Fairfax was called away to chase the King's army, a pursuit that ended at Naseby.

Title: Taken by surprise
Summary: Places seized by a raid, a trick or an attack at night.
Story:
Not every stronghold needed a siege. A small party moving fast, at night or in disguise, could take a place before its defenders knew they were under attack.

At Beeston Castle in December 1643 a handful of Royalists climbed the crag and took the "impregnable" castle. Dover Castle fell in 1642 to a dozen townsmen who scaled the cliffs and walls, and Shrewsbury, the King's base in the Welsh Marches, was taken by a night attack in February 1645.

Title: The defenders slipped away
Summary: Garrisons that abandoned their post or escaped before the end.
Story:
Some garrisons decided not to wait for the end. They marched out by night, burned their own quarters so the enemy could not use them, or gave up a town that could not be held.

The most famous escape was at Clonmel in 1650, where Hugh O'Neill's garrison inflicted Cromwell's worst losses in Ireland and then slipped away in the dark, leaving the townspeople to surrender. At Lydney the Royalists burned their own garrison rather than let it fall into enemy hands.

Title: Mines and petards
Summary: Sieges where the attackers tunnelled under the walls or blew in the gates.
Story:
Where cannon could not break a wall, attackers went under it. Miners dug a tunnel to the foundations, packed the end with gunpowder and blew a breach. Defenders listened for the digging, dug counter-mines and flooded the tunnels. A smaller version was the petard, a bell-shaped charge fixed to a gate and fired to blow it in.

The Lichfield write-up records the first explosive mine used in an English siege, set off by Prince Rupert's engineers in April 1643. Miners from the Forest of Dean worked at Gloucester, at York the defenders flooded the attackers' mines, and at Newcastle in October 1644 mines brought down the town walls before the Scots stormed in.

Title: When quarter was refused
Summary: Massacres and killings of prisoners after a siege.
Story:
"Quarter" meant sparing the life of an enemy who surrendered. It was the normal expectation, but it could be refused to a garrison that held out until it was stormed, and anger, revenge or religion sometimes overrode it altogether.

The worst killings in England came in 1643 to 1645: at Barthomley church, Hopton Castle, Bolton, Liverpool and Leicester, and at Shelford House near Newark. From October 1644 Parliament ordered that Irish soldiers captured in England be given no quarter, which is why Irishmen were hanged after the fall of Shrewsbury. The story ends with Cromwell's storming of Drogheda and Wexford in 1649, still the most bitterly remembered sieges of all.

Title: Slighted: what survives
Summary: Castles and houses deliberately ruined after their siege.
Story:
When the fighting was over, the winners made sure their enemies could never use a stronghold again. "Slighting" meant pulling down walls, blowing up towers and filling in ditches. In 1647 Parliament ordered the demolition of the castles that had been Royalist strongholds in the north, and many more followed.

That is why so many of the castles on this map are ruins today. Some were slighted almost to nothing, like Basing House and Bridgnorth; others got off lightly, like Stokesay, where only one wall came down.

Title: Newark and its outposts
Summary: The King's stronghold on the Trent, its ring of garrisons, and the raids launched from it.
Story:
Newark sat where the Great North Road crossed the Trent, and it held for the King from the start of the war to the end. It was besieged three times: in 1643, in 1644, when Prince Rupert's relief was one of the Royalists' greatest victories, and from November 1645, when Scottish and Parliamentarian armies closed in for good.

Around the town was a screen of fortified houses, including Shelford, Wiverton, Thurgarton and Norwell, with Belvoir Castle to the south-west. Newark's horsemen raided far beyond them, to Grantham, Melton Mowbray, Nottingham and Torksey. In the autumn of 1645 the outposts fell one by one; Shelford was stormed and most of its garrison killed.

Plague-ridden and short of food, Newark surrendered on 8 May 1646, and only on the King's order. Three days earlier Charles had given himself up to the Scots at Southwell, a few miles away.

Title: Oxford and its ring of garrisons
Summary: The King's wartime capital and the fortified houses that guarded its approaches.
Story:
After Edgehill in 1642, Charles I made Oxford his capital. To protect it he held a ring of garrisons on the roads and river crossings around it: Wallingford, Banbury, Donnington, Faringdon, Woodstock, Boarstall, Bletchingdon and others, each a few hours' ride away.

Reading was lost in April 1643. In 1644 the King slipped out of Oxford between two Parliamentarian armies, and in 1645 Fairfax's siege was called off to chase the King's army towards Naseby. In April 1645 Cromwell bluffed Bletchingdon House into surrendering, and its governor was shot by his own side for giving it up.

By the spring of 1646 the ring was being picked apart: Woodstock, Boarstall and Radcot Bridge fell, and Oxford surrendered on 24 June. Wallingford, its strongest outpost, held out a little longer.

Title: After Marston Moor
Summary: How the King's north fell apart after the battle of 2 July 1644.
Story:
On 2 July 1644 the armies of Parliament and the Scots routed Prince Rupert and the Marquess of Newcastle on Marston Moor, outside York. It was the largest battle of the civil wars. York surrendered a fortnight later, and Newcastle left England for exile.

With no field army left to come to their rescue, the King's garrisons across the north were picked off one after another: Tickhill, Sheffield, Staveley, Bolsover and Welbeck that summer, Knaresborough by Christmas, Newcastle upon Tyne stormed by the Scots in October. Others, like Carlisle, Helmsley, Skipton and Bolton Castle, held out for many months more, but the north was lost.

Title: After Naseby
Summary: The collapse of the King's cause in the year after 14 June 1645.
Story:
At Naseby on 14 June 1645, the New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell destroyed the King's main army. Leicester was retaken within four days. Fairfax then marched west, relieved Taunton, and began taking the King's strongholds one after another.

Bridgwater fell in July, Sherborne in August and Bristol in September, after which the King dismissed Prince Rupert. Cromwell took Winchester and stormed Basing House in October, and Fairfax pressed on into Devon. Far from the battle, garrisons such as Carlisle and Bolton Castle gave up once they knew no relief would ever come.

Title: Ports and the sea
Summary: Harbours, island forts and sieges decided by ships.
Story:
In 1642 the navy declared for Parliament. That one fact shaped many sieges: Hull, Plymouth and Lyme could be supplied and reinforced from the sea, however tightly the King's armies surrounded them, while Royalist ports such as Pendennis could be blockaded from both sides.

The King needed harbours to bring in men from Ireland and arms from the Continent, which made Bristol, Liverpool, Scarborough and the Welsh ports prizes worth fighting for. In 1648 part of the fleet changed sides and the castles of the Downs in Kent rose for the King. The last Royalist outposts of all were islands. Robert Blake's fleet took Scilly and Jersey in 1651, and Castle Cornet on Guernsey surrendered that December.

Title: Scotland and Ireland
Summary: The wars of the three kingdoms beyond England and Wales.
Story:
The civil wars began outside England, with the Scots' rising against Charles I's church reforms in 1639 and the Irish rebellion of 1641. Scotland had its own civil war in 1644 and 1645, when Royalist and Covenanter forces fought over castles across the Highlands.

After the King's execution, Cromwell took the New Model Army to Ireland in 1649. Drogheda, Wexford, Kilkenny and Clonmel fell within nine months. In 1650 he turned on Scotland, which had proclaimed Charles II king: after the battle of Dunbar, Edinburgh Castle, Tantallon, Stirling and Dunnottar were taken one by one; the last siege here, at Kildrummy, came in 1654.

Title: Besieged again and again
Summary: Places that were besieged more than once.
Story:
Some places could not escape the war. A strong castle or a town on a vital road or river crossing was worth taking, worth retaking, and worth taking again.

Basing House, Newark, Oxford, Lichfield, Taunton and Pontefract were each besieged three times. Others, such as Pembroke, Tenby and Scarborough, were fought over in the First Civil War and then again in 1648, when their own governors changed sides. Step through them to see how the same walls changed hands.

Title: Prince Rupert's trail
Summary: The King's nephew and cavalry general, from Bristol to his dismissal.
Story:
Prince Rupert of the Rhine, the King's nephew, was only 22 when the war began, but already a veteran of the wars in Europe. He became the Royalists' most feared commander, and his sieges were fast and often brutal: Cirencester, Birmingham and Lichfield in the first months of 1643, then the storming of Bristol that July.

In 1644 he relieved Newark and Lathom House, stormed Bolton and Liverpool on the march north, and broke the siege of York, only to be defeated at Marston Moor. His storming of Leicester in May 1645 came a fortnight before Naseby. When he surrendered Bristol that September, the King dismissed him.

Title: Sir Thomas Fairfax's trail
Summary: Parliament's best general, from the Yorkshire war to the New Model Army.
Story:
Sir Thomas Fairfax began the war fighting alongside his father in Yorkshire: Leeds, Wakefield and the defence of Hull in 1643, then the relief of Nantwich in January 1644, the siege of Lathom House, and Helmsley, where a musket ball broke his shoulder.

In 1645 he was made commander of the New Model Army. After Naseby he swept through the West Country, taking Bridgwater, Sherborne and Bristol, then Exeter, and in February 1646 Great Torrington, where the explosion in the church nearly killed him. He returned to Oxford to accept its surrender that June. In 1648 he ended the Second Civil War in the south-east with the siege of Colchester.

Follow the story to see his route drawn in, siege by siege.

Title: Oliver Cromwell's trail
Summary: From a cavalry colonel in the eastern counties to Ireland and Scotland.
Story:
In 1643 Oliver Cromwell was a cavalry colonel in the eastern counties, securing Lowestoft, Crowland and Burghley House and fighting at Grantham and Gainsborough. By 1645 he was second in command of the New Model Army, taking Bletchingdon, Bridgwater, Bristol, Winchester and Basing House.

In 1648 he crushed the rising in South Wales at Tenby, Chepstow and Pembroke. In 1649 he took the army to Ireland, where the storming of Drogheda and Wexford made his name hated, and in 1650 to Scotland, where Edinburgh Castle surrendered to him.

Follow the story to see his route drawn in, siege by siege.

Title: Sir William Waller's trail
Summary: Parliament's general in the south, nicknamed 'William the Conqueror'.
Story:
Sir William Waller won a string of quick successes in 1642 and 1643, taking Portsmouth, Farnham, Chichester and Highnam, which earned him the nickname "William the Conqueror". His luck turned in July 1643, when his siege of the King's western army at Devizes ended in defeat at Roundway Down.

His opponent in the West was Sir Ralph Hopton, an old friend; the two kept up a famous correspondence regretting that they had to fight each other. Waller failed at Basing House that November but recovered to storm Alton and retake Arundel. In 1644 he joined the attempt to trap the King in Oxford.

Follow the story to see his route drawn in, siege by siege.

Title: Sir Ralph Hopton's trail
Summary: The King's general in the West Country, and Waller's old friend.
Story:
Sir Ralph Hopton raised the King's army in Cornwall and led it east in 1643, fighting at Plymouth and at Lansdown outside Bath, where he was badly hurt by an exploding ammunition wagon. That winter he took Arundel Castle, only for his old friend and opponent Waller to win it back.

His last action was at Great Torrington in February 1646, where the gunpowder stored in the church exploded during the battle. Soon afterwards he surrendered the remains of the western army and went into exile.

Follow the story to see his route drawn in, siege by siege.

Title: Edward Massey's trail
Summary: The defender of Gloucester, and Parliament's fighting governor on the Severn.
Story:
Edward Massey was the young governor of Gloucester when the King besieged it in August 1643. He held the city for nearly four weeks until the Earl of Essex arrived to relieve it, one of the turning points of the war.

From Gloucester he fought a running war for the Forest of Dean and the Severn crossings: Highnam, Westbury, Newnham, Littledean, Beachley and Lydney. In 1645 he stormed Evesham, and that autumn his troops entered Tiverton on the way into Devon.

Follow the story to see his route drawn in, siege by siege.

Title: Sir William Brereton's trail
Summary: Parliament's commander in Cheshire and the north-west Midlands.
Story:
Sir William Brereton led Parliament's war in Cheshire and the counties around it. In 1643 he took Middlewich, Warrington and Stafford and fought for Lichfield; in 1644 he helped take Liverpool and relieve Montgomery.

His great task was Chester, the King's port for troops from Ireland. Brereton's blockade from September 1645 starved the city into surrender early in 1646, and he finished the war taking Lichfield Close, Dudley and Ludlow.

Follow the story to see his route drawn in, siege by siege.

Title: Turncoats and treachery
Summary: Bribes, betrayals and commanders who changed sides.
Story:
Loyalties were not always fixed. Some governors were bribed to open their gates, as at Hartlebury, where the surrender came with £3,000, and Chirk, which its owner bought back from its Royalist governor. Some fell to a plot from within: at Corfe Castle in 1646 one of the defending officers let in a hundred Parliamentarian soldiers disguised as reinforcements.

Others changed sides openly. Sir Hugh Cholmley took Scarborough over to the King in 1643, and in 1648 a wave of Parliamentarian commanders, unpaid and disillusioned, declared for the King at Pembroke, Tenby, Scarborough and Tynemouth. Several paid for it with their lives.

Title: Family homes at war
Summary: Country houses defended by their owners, their wives and their families.
Story:
Many of the places besieged in the civil wars were people's homes. Gentry families fortified their houses, garrisoned them for one side or the other, and often stayed inside when the enemy came.

With the men away, women frequently took command: Lady Brilliana Harley at Brampton Bryan, the Countess of Derby at Lathom, Lady Bankes at Corfe and Lady Blanche Arundell at Wardour, whose son later besieged his own family home to win it back. At Basing House the Marquis of Winchester scratched his motto, "Love Loyalty", on the windows. Families could lose everything, though some, like the Tattons at Wythenshawe, were later allowed to buy their houses back.

Title: Churches at war
Summary: Churches fortified, fought over, used as gun platforms or blown up.
Story:
In many villages and towns the church was the strongest building, and its tower the best lookout. Both sides used churches as forts, barracks, magazines and gun platforms, and more than one was the scene of the fiercest fighting of a siege.

Colonel Bolle was killed fighting in Alton church in 1643, and that same month villagers who had fled into the steeple at Barthomley were killed after being offered quarter. Lichfield Cathedral and its walled Close were besieged three times, and at Great Torrington in 1646 eighty barrels of gunpowder stored in the church exploded, blowing off the roof. Musket-ball holes and cannon-ball marks can still be seen at Hillesden and Old Malton.

Title: Townspeople caught up
Summary: The civilians who dug the defences, fed the soldiers, and suffered the sack.
Story:
A siege was not only soldiers' business. Townspeople dug earthworks, repaired breaches under fire and fed the garrison; at Plymouth men, women and children were made to dig trenches, and at Hereford the citizens patched the walls as fast as cannon broke them.

They also paid the price. Suburbs were burned to clear the ground, as at Gloucester. Plague and hunger followed long sieges, as at Chester and Newark. A town taken by storm, like Birmingham, Bolton or Leicester, could be plundered for days. By 1645 some country people had had enough and armed themselves as "Clubmen", demanding that both armies leave them alone.
